content: Narcissus pseudonarcissus, commonly referred to as the Wild Daffodil, is a perennial flowering plant belonging to the Amaryllidaceae family. It grows from a bulb and produces pale yellow flowers with a darker central trumpet. The plant's leaves are long, narrow, and slightly greyish in color, emerging from the base of the stem. This species is native to Western Europe, with its range extending from Spain and Portugal in the west to Germany in the east, and northward to England and Wales. It is frequently cultivated in gardens, and as a result, populations have become naturalized in various other parts of Europe. In the wild, the plant thrives in woodlands, grasslands, and rocky terrains. In Britain, native populations of the Wild Daffodil have significantly declined since the 19th century. This reduction is attributed to factors such as the intensification of agricultural practices, the clearance of woodlands, and the uprooting of bulbs for garden use. There are several subspecies of the Wild Daffodil, although the exact number varies depending on the classification system used by different authors. The large number of cultivated varieties further complicates the taxonomy of this species. One notable subspecies is the Tenby Daffodil (N. p. ssp. obvallaris), which is sometimes considered a separate species. This subspecies likely originated through cultivation but has since established itself in the wild, particularly in southwest Wales.
